title: Verdigris Analytics - model selection, context length & tool-calling scoping

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~48 min
Attendees: Maya T. (Redwood AE), Liam O. (Redwood SE), Priya N. (Redwood Solutions), Gina P. (Verdigris CTO), Rafael S. (ML Eng), Jamal R. (Security), Sofia M. (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough) : Customer is an analytics company with EU + US tenants, needs long-context document ingestion (financial reports + chat history), wants open models for licensing and fine-tuning flexibility, requires tool-calling to query internal DBs and trigger pipelines; high sensitivity re: GDPR and PCI-like controls.

[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll do quick intros then dive into model needs and infra constraints. Gina, want to kick off with business context?
[00:12] Gina (CTO): Yeah, thanks. Verdigris does time-series analytics for fintech and a lot of the work is ingesting large regulatory filings + customer chat logs, put them into a single conversational interface. So the context lengths get pretty big — like pulling in many months of logs plus long PDFs. We're exploring LLMs that can handle that natively or via retrieval, and we prefer open models to avoid vendor lock.
[00:34] Rafael (ML Eng): Also multilingual — English, Spanish, a decent amount of Portuguese and German, occasionally Japanese. We see code-switching inside chats. Latency matters for interactive use but we can tolerate a little more for complex doc summaries. Cost is a huge factor.
[00:50] Jamal (Security): From security side, we need SOC2 obviously, audit logs, SSO/SAML, role-based access, and importantly EU data residency for some customers. If we go private we need KMS/HSM integration.
[01:12] Maya: Perfect, that aligns with what people usually ask. Quick question — how big are the documents / how many tokens are we thinking per session?
[01:20] Rafael: Roughly 50k tokens typical, but some sessions approach 200k if you unfold a long financial filing plus chat. So we were thinking a model or a pipeline that can effectively manage ~256k token context, or at least fall back gracefully.
[01:35] Liam (SE): Got it. Two common approaches: 1) use a model with a native large context window (32k/128k/256k depending on model) or 2) retrieval + dynamic KV/prefix caching where you materialize context into a vector DB and stream relevant chunks in. Both have tradeoffs for latency and cost. With Redwood you can mix — route large, heavy requests to Dedicated or Private with higher memory and keep interactive queries on Hosted smaller models.
[02:10] Sofia (Product): When you say mix, do you mean automatic routing? Could we have the same API and different backends transparent to the product?
[02:19] Priya (Redwood): Yes — Redwood's routing policies let you decide by latency SLO, cost bucket, or tag. So the app calls the same endpoint; we can route by request size, user tier, or a header you set. If Dedicated capacity is busy it'll fallback to a cheaper hosted variant.
[02:38] Gina: About models — we want to evaluate open models. Which ones should we benchmark for our 256k use case?
[02:45] Liam: For open models with large-window variants: Llama-3 family has longer-window forks in the community, some vendors have 128k variants; Mistral has good quality/compute tradeoffs but you might need to work on longer windows via chunking + retrieval. There are also specialized long-context models — some third-party forks of Llama/RedPajama that claim 256k. We recommend starting with a matrix: 1) baseline high-quality 32k model (for latency compare), 2) 128k/256k long-window candidate, and 3) a smaller quantized model for embeddings and cheap reranking.
[03:26] Rafael: How reliable are those community long-window forks? We're concerned about hallucination when stitching.
[03:32] Liam: Good point — hallucination risk increases if you just concatenate. That's where KV cache and structured retrieval plus source attribution helps. Redwood Optimize has regression tests for prompt sets — you can detect quality regressions when switching quantization or model variants.
[03:48] Jamal: Regarding private deployment — what's the friction? We have EU-only clients that won't allow cross-border processing.
[03:56] Priya: For Private, we offer a customer-managed control plane, VPC peering, and on-prem options. We can integrate with your KMS/HSM for key custody and provide audit logs and SOC2 artifacts. The usual friction is network setup and initial sizing — for 256k windows you'll need GPUs with large VRAM or model slicing across servers. Redwood's Dedicated plan can reserve those pools as a middle ground.
[04:26] Gina: Cost ballpark? Dedicated for big-window models sounds expensive.
[04:30] Maya: We'll provide cost estimates — typically you trade off per-token compute vs throughput. We can model scenarios: full native 256k support on Dedicated, or hybrid: use retrieval + 32k models for 95% of calls and route 5% heavy queries to Dedicated. That often reduces unit cost by 3-5x.
[04:54] Rafael: Tool-calling — we need function calls to: 1) query an internal SQL analytics DB, 2) hit a vector DB for retrieval, 3) invoke a pipeline to re-run a job. How does Redwood enable safe tool-calling?
[05:07] Liam: We support structured function/tool-calling patterns in the API. You can define schemas for external calls; Redwood will capture the tool inputs/outputs in audit logs. For private mode, calls can be routed through an on-prem connector so the LLM never directly talks outside your network. You can also set allowlists and rate limits per tool.
[05:28] Sofia: Any issues with streaming responses when calling tools? We want partial answers while tools run.
[05:34] Priya: Streaming is supported. If a tool call is long-running, you can stream interim outputs; Redwood also supports async callbacks for webhook-style completions.
[05:42] Jamal: For compliance we need end-to-end encryption and to ensure tokens aren't persisted in logs for certain tenants. Is that doable?
[05:50] Priya: Yes — redaction and retention policies can be tenant-scoped. We can redact PHI and opt out of token retention; Private deployments can be configured so logs stay in your environment. KMS integration ensures keys are customer-managed.
[06:04] Gina: Back to models — what about multilingual quality? Some open models degrade in non-English.
[06:10] Liam: Right, quality varies. We usually run multilingual evals across your prompt sets. There are models that are stronger in EU languages; you might need targeted fine-tuning or instruction-tuning on your corpora. Redwood's eval pipeline can run side-by-side comparisons and show BLEU-like or semantic metrics plus cost/latency.
[06:30] Rafael: Will Redwood run benchmarks on our data or do we do it?
[06:34] Maya: We can run them together. Typical engagement: customer shares redacted prompt set + retrieval traces; Redwood runs a controlled benchmark on hosted or dedicated infra. If you want private infra we can assist with a transient on-prem benchmark plan.
[06:50] Gina: What's the turnaround? We need numbers for execs next week.
[06:54] Maya: We'll send a one-page benchmark plan today and a cost spreadsheet within 48 hours. For actual runs, 3-5 business days depending on queue.
[07:05] Rafael: For the 256k window test, do you need us to prepare full documents or a representative sampling?
[07:11] Liam: Representative sampling is good — include a few worst-case long filings plus conversation traces. Also include expected peak RPS and concurrency so we size Dedicated pools.
[07:22] Sofia: Any limitations on tool-calling for long-context workflows? For example, can we pass a 100k context and have the LLM call a function that uses a smaller extracted slice?
[07:32] Liam: Yes, that's a common pattern — you pass a large context or a pointer to it, extract the relevant chunk server-side, then call the tool with the extracted snippet. Redwood supports passing pointers/ids that map to cached vectors or prefix caches so you don't send massive payloads every time.
[07:49] Jamal: What about key management and HSM — does Redwood integrate with Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS?
[07:56] Priya: We integrate with common KMS providers (AWS,KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support HSM-backed flows for Private installs. We can document the integration steps and security model.
[08:08] Gina: Our legal team will ask about data residency and proof of processing location. Can you provide logs that show where inference ran?
[08:15] Maya: Yes — per-request metadata includes region, model variant, and node id. For Private deployments it's all in your control; for Hosted we can guarantee region constraints and show traces.
[08:26] Rafael: A few technical nitpicks: do you support mixed-precision quantization for long-window models? We want int8/4-bit to reduce VRAM for cheaper ops.
[08:38] Liam: We do. The runtime supports quantized kernels and can pick execution paths. But quantization can impact quality — Redwood Optimize recommends which layers to quantize and runs regression checks. For very long windows you sometimes need more memory, so model sharding + quantization is a typical approach.
[08:59] Sofia: Any customers doing the exact 200k+ token interactive flows on Redwood?
[09:05] Liam: A few fintech customers are experimenting with >100k. It's still early and often requires engineering tradeoffs (sharding, retrieval augmentation, or hybrid approach). We can share anonymized perf curves after NDA if useful.
[09:20] Gina: Competitors — we're also talking to OpenAI and Anthropic about embeddings and function-calling. How do you compare on cost?
[09:28] Maya: Broadly, open-model + Redwood hosting is cheaper per token vs fully managed proprietary endpoints, especially at scale. The trade is engineering for finetuning or maintaining model forks. Redwood reduces that burden by handling deployment, routing, and observability. We'll show a cost/latency comparison in the spreadsheet.
[09:45] Rafael: Regarding monitoring — we need per-tenant cost breakdowns and alerting on quality regressions.
[09:51] Priya: Console supports token-level cost, per-route dashboards, and eval-triggered regression alerts. You can attach prompt sets and baseline metrics and get notified when a model change leads to degraded output.
[10:05] Maya: Quick recap and next steps?
[10:09] Gina: We'd like: 1) benchmark plan and cost for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private targeted at our 256k scenario; 2) a short tech deck on tool-calling security and on-prem connectors; 3) schedule the benchmark session with your SE.
[10:22] Maya: Sounds good — we'll deliver those. Liam will follow up on the technical runbook. Priya will compile compliance docs.
[10:30] Rafael: I'll send a sample set of three worst-case documents and three conversation traces, redacted.
[10:36] Jamal: I'll send the redaction matrix and data residency list.
[10:41] Maya: Great. Anything else?
[10:44] Sofia: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.

(Background noise and brief crosstalk)
[10:55] End call.
